subject: Backtest hierarchy regression model with different priors

messages.author: ec64b10e28226ce1
messages.subject: Backtest hierarchy regression model with different priors
parts:
Hi all, I'm building a hierarchy model for revenue prediction  (model shown below). As you can see, model only consists of uninformative priors. The posterior for most of the beta's (beta_l2_1, beta_l2_2 etc.) all have some weird distributions while theoretically they should be gaussians. I was wondering whether that's because my posterior is mostly determined by the data as my prior is not very informative. 

As a result, I want to start with a simple parameter scan to see whether the posterior distribution would change, such as restrict the uniform distribution of of my sigma's to have a narrow range (instead of   sigma_beta_l3_0 ~ uniform(0,100), try   sigma_beta_l3_0 ~ uniform(0,10),   sigma_beta_l3_0 ~ uniform(0,5) etc.) Is there anyway I could pass in the distribution parameter as a variable (such as, try 3 numbers of b, run the model 3 times with uniform(0, b) ) instead of writing 3 text files with different b's ?

Thank you in advance!
Maggie

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  vector[N] y;
  vector[N] ant_spend;
  vector[N] unspent_ns;
  vector[N] cumul_revenue;
  int<lower=0> N_l1;  
  int<lower=0> N_l2;
  int<lower=0> N_l3;
  int<lower=1> ff_l1_num[N];  
  int<lower=1> ff_l2_num[N];
  int<lower=1> ff_l2_qtr_num[N];
  
  int<lower=0> N_new;
  vector[N_new] ant_spend_new;
  vector[N_new] unspent_ns_new;
  vector[N_new] cumul_revenue_new;
  int<lower=1> ff_l2_qtr_num_new[N_new];
  
  }
  parameters {
  real beta_0;
  real beta_1;
  real beta_2;
  real beta_3;
  real<lower=0> sigma_y;
  real<lower=0> sigma_beta_l1_0;
  real<lower=0> sigma_beta_l1_1;
  real<lower=0> sigma_beta_l1_2;
  real<lower=0> sigma_beta_l1_3;  
  real<lower=0> sigma_beta_l2_0;
  real<lower=0> sigma_beta_l2_1;
  real<lower=0> sigma_beta_l2_2;
  real<lower=0> sigma_beta_l2_3;
  real<lower=0> sigma_beta_l3_0;  
  real<lower=0> sigma_beta_l3_1;  
  real<lower=0> sigma_beta_l3_2;
  real<lower=0> sigma_beta_l3_3;
  vector[N_l1] beta_l1_0;
  vector[N_l1] beta_l1_1;
  vector[N_l1] beta_l1_2;
  vector[N_l1] beta_l1_3;   
  vector[N_l2] beta_l2_0;
  vector[N_l2] beta_l2_1;
  vector[N_l2] beta_l2_2;
  vector[N_l2] beta_l2_3;  
  vector[N_l3] beta_l3_0;  
  vector[N_l3] beta_l3_1;
  vector[N_l3] beta_l3_2;
  vector[N_l3] beta_l3_3;
  
  }
  transformed parameters {
  vector[N] y_hat;
  for (i in 1:N)
  y_hat[i] <- beta_l3_0[ff_l2_qtr_num[i]] + beta_l3_1[ff_l2_qtr_num[i]] * ant_spend[i] + beta_l3_2[ff_l2_qtr_num[i]] * cumul_revenue[i] + beta_l3_3[ff_l2_qtr_num[i]] * unspent_ns[i];
  }
  
  model {
  sigma_y ~ uniform(0, 100);
  sigma_beta_l1_0 ~ uniform(0,100);
  sigma_beta_l2_0 ~ uniform(0,100);
  sigma_beta_l3_0 ~ uniform(0,100);  
  beta_0 ~ normal(0,1);
  beta_l1_0 ~ normal(beta_0, sigma_beta_l1_0);
  for (n_l2 in 1:N_l2)
  beta_l2_0[n_l2] ~ normal(beta_l1_0[ff_l1_num[n_l2]], sigma_beta_l2_0);
  for (n_l3 in 1:N_l3)
  beta_l3_0[n_l3] ~ normal(beta_l2_0[ff_l2_num[n_l3]], sigma_beta_l3_0);
  
  sigma_beta_l1_1 ~ uniform(0,100);
  sigma_beta_l2_1 ~ uniform(0,100);
  sigma_beta_l3_1 ~ uniform(0,100);  
  beta_1 ~ normal(0,1);
  beta_l1_1 ~ normal(beta_1, sigma_beta_l1_1);
  for (n_l2 in 1:N_l2)
  beta_l2_1[n_l2] ~ normal(beta_l1_1[ff_l1_num[n_l2]], sigma_beta_l2_1);
  for (n_l3 in 1:N_l3)
  beta_l3_1[n_l3] ~ normal(beta_l2_1[ff_l2_num[n_l3]], sigma_beta_l3_1);
  
  sigma_beta_l1_2 ~ uniform(0,100);
  sigma_beta_l2_2 ~ uniform(0,100);
  sigma_beta_l3_2 ~ uniform(0,100);  
  beta_2 ~ normal(0,1);
  beta_l1_2 ~ normal(beta_2, sigma_beta_l1_2);
  for (n_l2 in 1:N_l2)
  beta_l2_2[n_l2] ~ normal(beta_l1_2[ff_l1_num[n_l2]], sigma_beta_l2_2);
  for (n_l3 in 1:N_l3)
  beta_l3_2[n_l3] ~ normal(beta_l2_2[ff_l2_num[n_l3]], sigma_beta_l3_2);  
  
  sigma_beta_l1_3 ~ uniform(0,100);  
  sigma_beta_l2_3 ~ uniform(0,100);
  sigma_beta_l3_3 ~ uniform(0,100);  
  beta_3 ~ normal(0,1);
  beta_l1_3 ~ normal(beta_3, sigma_beta_l1_3);
  for (n_l2 in 1:N_l2)
  beta_l2_3[n_l2] ~ normal(beta_l1_3[ff_l1_num[n_l2]], sigma_beta_l2_3);
  for (n_l3 in 1:N_l3)
  beta_l3_3[n_l3] ~ normal(beta_l2_3[ff_l2_num[n_l3]], sigma_beta_l3_3);  
  
  y ~ normal(y_hat, sigma_y); 
  }
  generated quantities {
  vector[N] log_lik;
  vector[N_new] rev_pred;
  
  for (i in 1:N) log_lik[i] <- normal_log(y[i], y_hat[i], sigma_y);
  for (j in 1:N_new) rev_pred[j] <- normal_rng(beta_l3_0[ff_l2_qtr_num_new[j]] + 
  beta_l3_1[ff_l2_qtr_num_new[j]] * ant_spend_new[j] + 
  beta_l3_2[ff_l2_qtr_num_new[j]] * cumul_revenue_new[j] +
  beta_l3_3[ff_l2_qtr_num_new[j]] * unspent_ns_new[j], sigma_y); 
  }

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Backtest hierarchy regression model with different priors
parts:
> On May 3, 2016, at 3:37 PM, maggiec via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
>
> Hi all, I'm building a hierarchy model for revenue prediction (model shown below). As you can see, model only consists of uninformative priors. The posterior for most of the beta's (beta_l2_1, beta_l2_2 etc.) all have some weird distributions while theoretically they should be gaussians.

What makes you think the posteriors should be Gaussians? It's
not like you're laying out a conjugate model.
> I was wondering whether that's because my posterior is mostly determined by the data as my prior is not very informative.

Just because your prior isn't "informative" doesn't mean it
won't have a big impact on the posterior. See all of Gelman's
papers cited in our manual, for examples.

We do not recommend interval priors on parameters that don't
mathematically require it (say a correlation parameter falling
between -1 and 1). If you insist on those priors, you should declare
sigma with <lower=0, upper=100>, because parameters should have
support (finite log density) for any value of parameters meeting the
constraints.

> As a result, I want to start with a simple parameter scan to see whether the posterior distribution would change, such as restrict the uniform distribution of of my sigma's to have a narrow range (instead of sigma_beta_l3_0 ~ uniform(0,100), try sigma_beta_l3_0 ~ uniform(0,10), sigma_beta_l3_0 ~ uniform(0,5) etc.) Is there anyway I could pass in the distribution parameter as a variable (such as, try 3 numbers of b, run the model 3 times with uniform(0, b) ) instead of writing 3 text files with different b's ?

Just declare b as data and pass in values. Just make sure
to put b in the bounds for sigma. But really, we wouldn't
recommend doing this.

You might want to check out all the posterior predictive checking
material in the Gelman and Hill regression book or the Gelman et al.
Bayesian Data Analysis book, or in my case study, which I wrote largely
to illustrate these principles:

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/pool-binary-trials.html

What you're talking about is a sensitivity analysis on the priors.
That's good, but it's only part of the story.

Stan implements both arrays and vectors so you don't have to do this
kind of cut-and-paste:

> real beta_1;
> real beta_2;
> real beta_3;

You can just have

real beta[3];

Then you can vectorize the prior and the model will be about 1/3 as
long and more efficient.

I would also strongly suggest indenting the code for readability just
like any other code.

This

can be vectorized as

beta_l2_0 ~ normal(beta_l1_0[ff_l1_num], sigma_beta_l2_0);


- Bob
